Dialogue 05: Successful login does not prove invoice posting works
Original fictional setting: The integration team has tested employee login to the new identity platform successfully. A scheduled invoice-posting job still uses a legacy service account and has not passed an end-to-end test on the new setup. IT lead Fatima and integration consultant Eric review the planned retirement of the legacy identity service. No go-live approval is supplied, and broad shared-administrator access is not an approved workaround.
Professional roles: Eric / Fatima
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Eric: Employee login passed on the new platform. Can we tell the sponsor that the old identity service is ready to retire?
Fatima: Not yet. That single sign-on test covers employee access, not every automated job using the existing environment.
Eric: The finance workstream mentioned that invoice posting runs on a schedule rather than through a person signing in.
Fatima: Correct. It still uses a legacy service account, and that dependency has not been resolved in the new setup.
Eric: If we retire the old identity service before addressing it, the business impact could be failed invoice posting.
Fatima: That is the legacy dependency the sponsor needs to understand in operational terms.
Eric: We need to test the actual invoice process from its start through the expected output, not just repeat the login test.
Fatima: Yes. The end-to-end test must use the agreed requirements and authorized test arrangements.
Eric: Finance also needs to verify that the resulting records match the expected transactions and totals.
Fatima: Include that reconciliation in the acceptance evidence. A job reporting success does not by itself prove that every output is correct.
Eric: Someone suggested sharing a broad administrator account until the integration team has more time to solve the issue.
Fatima: That is not approved. Maintain least privilege and use the actual access-review process for an appropriate solution.
Eric: The cutover window is already in the calendar, but the remaining tests and approvals have not been completed.
Fatima: Then the go/no-go decision remains separate from the scheduled window. We must report the unresolved facts before that review.
Eric: We should also know what happens if the approved transition starts and the business checks fail.
Fatima: The rollback plan needs its actual owner, conditions, and verified feasibility rather than a vague promise to undo everything.
Eric: I will align the IT and finance updates so one does not say complete while the other still reports an untested process.
Fatima: Good. User acceptance testing should reflect the business outcome, not just a successful technical component.
Eric: The sponsor update will state that login passed, invoice posting remains dependent on the old service, and the decision is pending.
Fatima: That makes data integrity and continuity visible without bypassing controls, inventing approval, or treating the new platform's appearance as evidence that the migration is complete.
Vocabulary in this exchange: workstream: Defined area of coordinated integration work. / dependency: Requirement or preceding activity on which another task relies. / cutover: Controlled transition from one operating setup to another. / single sign-on: Authentication arrangement allowing access across approved services. / service account: Identity used by an application or automated process. / least privilege: Limiting access to what is needed for the authorized task.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: New ownership does not rewrite every invoice instruction
Original fictional setting: After the acquisition, customer contact Morgan receives a new logo announcement and a separate email asking for payment to a new bank account. Under the supplied approved transition plan, the existing US subsidiary remains the invoicing entity and payment instructions have not been changed. Account lead Sofia and integration consultant Daniel must verify the unexpected email through established channels and avoid sending unapproved new instructions.
Professional roles: Sofia / Daniel
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Sofia: A customer received our new logo announcement and then an email asking them to pay a different bank account. They assume both are part of integration.
Daniel: Separate the brand transition from the payment request. The approved plan has not changed the remittance instructions.
Sofia: The customer also asks whether the overseas parent now replaces the US subsidiary on every invoice.
Daniel: Under the approved plan, the invoicing entity remains the existing US subsidiary. We should not infer a substitution from the acquisition announcement.
Sofia: Their contract names that subsidiary too, but any actual transfer question needs the appropriate legal review.
Daniel: Correct. The contracting entity and its obligations should be described from the actual records, not a simplified group label.
Sofia: For the bank-account email, we should verify through the contact route already established in the relationship.
Daniel: Yes. Use independent verification rather than relying on a new phone number printed in that same email.
Sofia: I will not send a replacement account number or ask the customer to choose between the two sets of instructions.
Daniel: Good. Payment redirection needs the actual controlled process and verified authorization.
Sofia: The logo and correct account-manager name make the email look convincing, but those details do not establish that it is genuine.
Daniel: That is why business email compromise is relevant during a transition. A plausible integration story should not bypass the controls.
Sofia: The customer may also need to update its supplier record, but we should give only approved entity information.
Daniel: Exactly. Any vendor master change should follow the customer's and our actual verification requirements.
Sofia: Our immediate response can explain that the existing approved payment instructions remain in place while the unexpected request is checked.
Daniel: That protects customer continuity without pretending that every integration question is already resolved.
Sofia: I will coordinate the account response with finance and the authorized security or fraud-reporting contact, preserving the message as required.
Daniel: Also align the customer-facing notice so customers do not receive conflicting instructions from sales, finance, and the integration team.
Sofia: The account owner and support route remain clear, and any future approved change will use the actual notice and verification process.
Daniel: Record that in the commercial continuity plan. New ownership is not a reason to improvise a contract transfer or a bank-account change.
Vocabulary in this exchange: customer continuity: Maintenance of customer service and obligations during transition. / contracting entity: Legal person entering the relevant customer agreement. / invoicing entity: Entity issuing the invoice under the actual arrangement. / brand transition: Change in external name or visual presentation. / vendor master: Customer or company record containing supplier details. / independent verification: Check using a trusted source separate from the unverified request.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: Annual run rate is not money already realized
Original fictional setting: A fictional procurement change saves USD 50,000 per month for three completed months against the agreed baseline. Gross realized savings are USD 150,000. A one-time integration cost of USD 90,000 belongs to the same reporting period and defined cash basis, giving USD 60,000 net realized benefit. Annualizing the monthly saving gives a USD 600,000 run rate, not a realized full-year result. IT and procurement both list the same saving in their workstream reports.
Professional roles: Oscar / Nina
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Oscar: The procurement change saves fifty thousand dollars a month, so I reported six hundred thousand as realized integration savings.
Nina: That is the annualized run-rate saving, not the completed-period result. We have three months of actual savings in the supplied record.
Oscar: Three times fifty thousand gives one hundred fifty thousand of gross savings for those completed months.
Nina: Correct. That is the in-period realization before the related cost included in this reporting basis.
Oscar: The one-time implementation expense was ninety thousand in the same period, and the report uses the stated cash basis.
Nina: Then include the one-time integration cost rather than letting the headline imply the change was free to deliver.
Oscar: The net realized benefit is therefore sixty thousand, even though the monthly saving could continue beyond this quarter.
Nina: Exactly. The net benefit and the annual run rate are useful but different measures.
Oscar: I also noticed that IT listed the same vendor reduction in its workstream total because it helped remove duplicate licenses.
Nina: We need to prevent double counting. Acknowledging both teams does not create two separate economic benefits.
Oscar: We can assign one shared record to the saving and show IT and procurement as contributors.
Nina: Put that in the benefit register, with a single accountable owner for assembling and validating the evidence.
Oscar: We should also identify the reference cost we compared against, so the saving is not based on an unexplained estimate.
Nina: Yes. The agreed baseline and any adjustments need to be traceable rather than reconstructed after the result is announced.
Oscar: If a planned future expense never occurs, should we record that in the same way as this reduction in an existing cost?
Nina: Not automatically. Cost avoidance needs its own definition and evidence under the reporting methodology.
Oscar: I will show the monthly rate, actual months, gross amount, included cost, and net result in the steering pack.
Nina: That creates a clear benefit bridge, with the six-hundred-thousand annualization labeled separately.
Oscar: The revised headline will acknowledge the ongoing opportunity without saying that a full year's saving has already been achieved.
Nina: Good. Complete the required finance validation and retain the evidence, so the report is credible rather than merely larger.
Vocabulary in this exchange: workstream: Defined area of coordinated integration work. / baseline: Agreed reference against which a change is measured. / net benefit: Benefit after the specified costs on the defined basis. / run-rate saving: Annualized or other normalized saving based on a stated current rate. / in-period realization: Benefit actually achieved within the stated reporting period. / one-time integration cost: Nonrecurring transition cost under the stated classification.
END REFERENCE

Nina: Yes. The agreed baseline and any adjustments need to be traceable rather than reconstructed after the result is announced.
Oscar: If a planned future expense never occurs, should we record that in the same way as this reduction in an existing cost?
Nina: Not automatically. Cost avoidance needs its own definition and evidence under the reporting methodology.
Oscar: I will show the monthly rate, actual months, gross amount, included cost, and net result in the steering pack.
Nina: That creates a clear benefit bridge, with the six-hundred-thousand annualization labeled separately.
Oscar: The revised headline will acknowledge the ongoing opportunity without saying that a full year's saving has already been achieved.
Nina: Good. Complete the required finance validation and retain the evidence, so the report is credible rather than merely larger.
Vocabulary in this exchange: workstream: Defined area of coordinated integration work. / baseline: Agreed reference against which a change is measured. / net benefit: Benefit after the specified costs on the defined basis. / run-rate saving: Annualized or other normalized saving based on a stated current rate. / in-period realization: Benefit actually achieved within the stated reporting period. / one-time integration cost: Nonrecurring transition cost under the stated classification.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 08: An assigned issue is not a resolved issue
Original fictional setting: The fictional handover plan requires five consecutive stable operating days before service acceptance. The new process has completed two stable days. A reporting defect remains open but has an identified finance owner. Sponsor Morgan wants the integration workstream closed immediately. Consultant Arjun explains the unmet acceptance condition and prepares the operational ownership, support, and open-item records without claiming that assignment means resolution.
Professional roles: Morgan / Arjun
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Morgan: The process has worked for two days, and finance owns the remaining reporting issue. Can we close the workstream today?
Arjun: The acceptance criteria specify five consecutive stable days. We have completed two, not the required five.
Morgan: I do not want the integration team to remain indefinitely just because one minor report still needs attention.
Arjun: We can plan the handover, but service acceptance and closure need their actual evidence and authority.
Morgan: The finance lead has accepted responsibility for the report. Does that at least mean we can mark the defect closed?
Arjun: No. The defect backlog should show it as open with an owner, next action, and review route.
Morgan: The receiving team also needs to know how the new process works and whom to contact when something fails.
Arjun: That is knowledge transfer, not just a document email. We need to check that the operational team can use the material.
Morgan: We have a draft procedure, but the escalation contact still points to a consultant who leaves next week.
Arjun: Then the runbook needs a workable ongoing contact before we describe the support arrangement as complete.
Morgan: We should confirm the hours and scope of support instead of assuming the receiving team provides the same transition coverage.
Arjun: Yes. Support coverage and the operating resources need explicit agreement.
Morgan: Could we say the handover is prepared while leaving acceptance pending until the stated conditions are met?
Arjun: That is accurate. Ownership transfer still needs the receiving role's actual acceptance and the required record.
Morgan: If leadership wants an exception to the five-day condition, it should be a visible decision through the specified authority.
Arjun: Correct. Do not hide an open risk by changing the status label. Any exception needs its actual approval and conditions.
Morgan: I will tell the sponsor group that handover preparation is progressing, but the operating evidence does not yet meet the criterion.
Arjun: Include that distinction in the closure report, along with the reporting defect and the named operational responsibilities.
Morgan: After acceptance, we should review whether the integration achieved its intended service and value outcomes, not just whether the project ended.
Arjun: Schedule the post-integration review. That keeps attention on the ongoing business result without declaring unfinished work complete today.
Vocabulary in this exchange: workstream: Defined area of coordinated integration work. / explicit agreement: Clearly stated acceptance rather than inferred assent. / acceptance criteria: Conditions that must be met for the stated acceptance decision. / service acceptance: Formal acceptance of an operational service under the actual process. / knowledge transfer: Handover of information and practical capability to another team. / runbook: Operational instructions and responsibilities for recurring tasks or incidents.
END REFERENCE

Name each role, establish an actual work problem, and let the exchange progress through questions, clarification, competing constraints and a credible next step or explicitly unresolved issue. Use the occupation's natural nomenclature and register. Avoid an interview between a teacher and a learner, generic small talk, and inserting a glossary definition into every reply. Explain specialist terms outside the dialogue instead.
4. After the script, explain five useful expressions in context and identify two grammar or register choices. Give three four-choice questions about the speakers' reasoning, with exactly one answer supported by the dialogue. Wait for my selections, then explain why each answer fits and why its alternatives fail. Add a role-switch reading using the supplied script; do not ask for an essay or invented written reply.
5. Before presenting a script, check names, numbers, chronology, roles and terminology for consistency. Label invented facts and acknowledge uncertain specialist usage. If I requested all six, deliver one complete script at a time and wait for "next". Make each scenario materially different.

Professional audience: M&A integration consultants, integration managers, workstream leads, post-acquisition specialists

Lesson 01: Protecting Day 1 business continuity
Original fictional case: An overseas buyer completed the acquisition of a fictional US business on Friday. On Monday, employees must be able to enter the site, receive support, and follow the existing approved payroll process. The shared HR platform is not ready, and no immediate payroll migration is authorized. Integration consultant Aya and US operations lead Marcus prioritize continuity and identify the later migration work separately.
Language workshop: The deal closed; the payroll process did not move overnight
Communication goal: Separate legal closing, immediate operating needs, and later integration milestones.
Language guidance: Legal close and completed integration are different. The supplied Monday plan preserves the existing payroll process; it does not authorize immediate migration.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Closing is complete; platform integration is not. / Which services must work when employees arrive on Monday? / Payroll remains on the existing approved process. / Migration depends on readiness checks and the required authorization. / Who owns continuity if the new platform is delayed? / This is the temporary operating arrangement, not the final design. / Employees need one clear support route for the transition. / We are ready for the stated Day 1 scope, not every future integration change. / Are you asking about the finding or the next step? / Please correct me if I have misunderstood that detail. / That is what the current record says; it has not been independently confirmed. / That is a possibility, not an agreed outcome. / That decision sits outside my authority. / Who is responsible for that specific next step? / Let me restate the distinction more clearly. / We agree on the action, the owner, and the point for review.
Vocabulary: legal close: Completion of the transaction under its actual closing requirements. / Day 1 readiness: Preparedness for required operations immediately after closing. / business continuity: Ability to sustain required operations through change or disruption. / integration management office: Team coordinating integration governance and workstreams. / workstream: Defined area of coordinated integration work. / critical service: Service whose interruption materially affects required operations. / minimum operating requirement: Condition needed for the specified operation to function. / transition service agreement: Contract for specified temporary support during a transition. / standalone capability: Ability to perform a function without the temporary support being replaced. / interim operating model: Temporary arrangement used during transition. / target operating model: Intended future arrangement of roles, processes, and systems. / readiness checkpoint: Defined review of whether prerequisites are met. / dependency: Requirement or preceding activity on which another task relies. / continuity owner: Person accountable for keeping a specified operation functioning. / hypercare: Time-limited heightened support after a transition. / service desk: Contact function handling user support requests. / critical-path item: Task whose timing can constrain the overall sequence. / Day 100 milestone: Stated later integration target, not a universal legal deadline. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange and distinguish closed, ready for Day 1, interim, and fully integrated. Switch roles and deliver the Monday message without announcing an unauthorized payroll change. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Aya: Integration consultant / Marcus: US operations lead
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: The employee portal has new branding, but the approved support process remains unchanged. The shared support platform has not launched.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Aya: Before the later migration, we can review the actual evidence that the required tests and authorizations are complete.
Marcus: That is the purpose of a readiness checkpoint. A target date should not substitute for verified readiness.
Aya: I will revise the message: the transaction has closed, immediate operations continue under the stated plan, and migration work remains scheduled for review.
Marcus: Good. The target operating model can remain our destination without being announced as a completed fact on the first working day.
END REFERENCE
